episode_title: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier's Girlfriend

stories.topic: The German Tank Problem: Statisticians vs the Brigadier's Girlfriend
stories.summary: Late in World War II the Allies needed to know whether Germany's new heavy tanks were a few showpieces or were being mass-produced. Spies, the people who 'knew the girlfriend of some brigadier', reported around 1,500 tanks a month. Statisticians used a different source: the serial numbers on tanks destroyed in battle. The methodical Germans numbered their tanks in sequence. So if you have seen, say, 24, 74 and 90, you should not conclude there are only 90 tanks. You take the average gap between the observed numbers and add it to the highest one. Their estimate was about 200 a month. When the Allies examined German production records after the war, the statisticians turned out to be right and the spies wrong.
stories.insight: Careful reasoning about how data is generated can beat apparently privileged insider information. A simple formula applied to the right structure outperformed gossip. Germany's orderly numbering itself became an intelligence leak; as Ajay notes, it would have been harder if every number had been randomized.
stories.quote: And after the war ended, when the Allies went and did the postmortem inside the German production records, it turned out that basically the statisticians were right and the humint was wrong.

stories.topic: The Naive Question That Led to the Cramér-Rao Bound
stories.summary: Ajay began his PhD without ever having studied probability or statistics, so he was made to take a fourth-year undergraduate econometrics class taught by Dennis Aigner. Aigner opened with a 'helicopter tour' of all of statistics that swept Ajay away. As Aigner showed how one estimator could be improved, and then improved again, Ajay asked whether there had to be a theoretical limit. Aigner replied that an Indian had asked exactly that question and answered it. The answer is the Cramér-Rao lower bound.
stories.insight: Admitting a gap in your knowledge is how you close it ('All gaps are overcomable'). A beginner's obvious question can lead straight to a field's foundational result, and in this case that result was proved by a young Indian in Calcutta.
stories.quote: And I put up my hand and I said that surely you can't keep going forever, that there will be a limit, there will be a theoretical limit on how good an estimator can get. And he said there was an Indian guy who asked that question and he got the answer, and that is the Cramér-Rao lower bound.

stories.topic: CR Rao in Calcutta, and Fisher's Decency
stories.summary: CR Rao was born in 1920. He came from Andhra Pradesh to Calcutta as an ordinary student at PC Mahalanobis's Indian Statistical Institute (ISI). This was before independence, so there was no government money, and Mahalanobis often funded the institute himself. Cut off from the European mainstream, Rao produced two of the handful of greatest results in 20th-century statistics: the Cramér-Rao lower bound in 1943, and the Rao-Blackwell theorem, which is a technique for making an estimator one step better. Each was discovered independently of the other person named in it. Ajay asked the mathematician Rajeeva Karandikar how Rao's name survived, given how easily Indian work gets ignored. The answer was Ronald Fisher. Fisher visited ISI, understood the results and started calling them by the joint names. Ajay compares this to the Royal Society presenting Darwin and Wallace together.
stories.insight: World-class work can come from an isolated outpost, but recognition depends on the decency of the people who control the field. Without Fisher, work done in Calcutta in 1943, with no internet, could simply have disappeared. Ajay says Indian work is still routinely ignored and later claimed by others, and that this has happened to him.
stories.quote: This is the decency of Fisher that Fisher started calling it the Rao-Blackwell Theorem. Fisher started calling it the Cramér-Rao lower bound. And suddenly for the whole world, it became Rao's work.

stories.topic: How ISI's Head Start Was Squandered
stories.summary: Having one CR Rao convinced a whole generation at ISI that 'this is a game we can play'. ISI was world-class, and its journal Sankhya was respected internationally and stocked by libraries everywhere. That early lead did not build into anything larger. In the 1970s and 80s the frontier moved from mathematical statistics, which proves theorems about closed-form estimators, to computational statistics. Bradley Efron's bootstrap in 1979 was one of the key innovations. In computational statistics an estimator can be an algorithm, which requires combining statistics with computer science. India's statistics community stuck to theorem-proving and missed the shift that grew into today's data-science revolution.
stories.insight: Being at the frontier once guarantees nothing. Fields reinvent themselves, and communities that don't follow get left behind. Ajay also sees a deeper problem: the way Indian state-funded research institutions are managed seems incompatible with excellence.
stories.quote: But the Indian statistics community didn't turn on the dime and reinvent themselves. And that's just a pity.

stories.topic: CRRao.jl: A Name as a Commitment Device
stories.summary: At XKDR Forum and the Chennai Mathematical Institute, Ajay's colleague Sourish Das leads a Julia package. It gives one uniform way to call many kinds of estimators, from linear regression to random forests, in either frequentist or Bayesian form. While names were being debated, Sourish proposed calling it CRRao.jl as a 'commitment device', a way to kick themselves into doing it well. Later CR Rao's daughter emailed to say she had shown her father the package and he had smiled.
stories.insight: Naming your work after a hero is a public promise to meet his standard. That smile was, in Ajay's words, the closest he ever came to the greatness of CR Rao.
stories.quote: We got an email from CR Rao's daughter that somehow she became aware that we had built this package and she said that she showed it to him and he smiled. Okay, so that is the closest that I ever came to the greatness that is CR Rao.

stories.topic: Abraham Wald and the Missing Bullets
stories.summary: Around 1942 Abraham Wald was drafted into a wartime research group so brilliant that someone quipped Milton Friedman was the fourth smartest person in the room. Wald did not have security clearance. The joke went that a secretary stood beside him and took away each sheet as soon as he finished writing it. The group was asked how to strengthen planes that came back riddled with bullets. Returning planes had more holes in the fuselage than in the engine, so the obvious plan was to reinforce the fuselage. Wald asked where the missing bullets were. If hits are spread fairly evenly, the missing ones struck the planes that never came back. So the engine, the part with the fewest holes on returning planes, was the part to protect.
stories.insight: The data you can see has been filtered by survival, and the most important evidence is often what is absent. Amit connects this to Ricky Ponting, who said he carried a map of the gaps in the field rather than of the fielders.
stories.quote: Where are the missing bullets? The missing bullets are in the planes that went down. So it is the engine that you need to protect.

stories.summary: Amit once wrote a column built on this scam. You contact 1,000 cricket bettors and offer free tips. You tell 500 of them India will win the next India–Sri Lanka match and tell the other 500 that Sri Lanka will. Whatever happens, you then split the group you got right in half and repeat. After a few rounds, a dozen or so people have seen you call five or six results in a row, and they will gladly pay you. Mutual funds can work the same way: run a family of funds following random strategies, and by sheer luck one of them will show a brilliant five- or six-year record.
stories.insight: A great track record means nothing until you know how many attempts failed and vanished. Selection can look exactly like skill.
stories.quote: You can just randomly make them do different things and by sheer dumb luck, one will come out on top. But it doesn't mean that that is a correct strategy. Perhaps it just got lucky.

stories.topic: How Many Lives Does It Take to Kill a Factory?
stories.summary: Allied bombers flew from Britain to hit German factories and refineries, facing German fighters and 88mm anti-aircraft guns. Pilots wanted to fly at 20,000 feet, above the guns. But WWII bombs, falling under gravity, could land kilometres off target, so very few hit from that height. At 6,000 feet more crews would be shot down, but far more bombs would hit. The statisticians, including a young Robert McNamara, ignored how frightening each altitude felt. They calculated how many airmen died for each factory destroyed, and the answer was 6,000 feet. When the pilots were told, they were in uproar. Along the way Ajay explains that the phrase 'a wing and a prayer' comes from crippled bombers gliding home with their engines shot out.
stories.insight: Choosing the right thing to measure can overturn intuition. The option that looks deadlier for each flight can cost fewer lives overall. Refusing to put numbers on a hard trade-off does not make it go away.
stories.quote: And Curtis LeMay and Robert McNamara said, we love you more than life itself, but we want fewer of you to die. And the way to do it is to go at 6,000 because we are counting how many of you die per unit factory killed.

stories.summary: Amit adds a sad coda. Abraham Wald died in 1950, aged 48, in an Air India crash in India, along with his wife. He had just given a talk at ISI in Calcutta and was travelling to a statistics congress in Bangalore.
stories.insight: The story comes full circle: the wartime statisticians and the ISI world of Mahalanobis and Rao were closely connected, and Calcutta was then a stop for the world's best statisticians.
stories.quote: And this again brings us a full circle back to the ISI because he died in India.

stories.topic: Mahalanobis: Genius Trapped by His Own Genius
stories.summary: Mahalanobis trained in physics. On the voyage back to India he was given volumes of the statistics journal Biometrika, and he arrived home in love with statistics. He taught physics at Presidency College before founding ISI. Reading from Nikhil Menon's Planning Democracy, Amit describes a stern, prim workaholic with coconut-oiled hair who showed affection only to his pets. He was a proud polymath, 'a physicist by training, statistician by intellect, and planner by conviction', who 'thought he knew best in practically every matter'. He made staff and students record their daily activities in a diary. Milton Friedman warned that able mathematicians, used to a field of absolutes, become dangerous when they turn to economic planning. Another account, which Amit attributes to Hannah Arendt, calls him domineering and vain, a Bengali aristocrat moving towards Stalinist-style authoritarianism.
stories.insight: The certainty and control that make a brilliant scientist and institution-builder can turn into hubris when applied to a messy society. Ajay calls this a recurring theme: the precision of science and engineering leaves many successful people unprepared for the real world.
stories.quote: A man who is a genius, but in a sense is also trapped by his own genius into a hubris and an arrogance that doesn't serve him so well.

stories.topic: The 1944 Jute Showdown: Sampling vs Counting
stories.summary: In 1944 random sample surveys were not yet widely accepted anywhere in the world, and there were calls to abandon them. The Bengal government settled the dispute with a contest over jute. Traditional plot-by-plot counting and ISI's random sample survey were run at the same time, and both were checked against official jute sales figures. The count was off by 16.6%. The sample survey was off by only 0.3%, and it cost a tenth as much.
stories.insight: A well-designed sample can beat a brute-force count on accuracy and cost at the same time. A clean head-to-head test was what finally won the argument for ISI.
stories.quote: The cumbersome enumeration or counting carried out by the government turned out to be off the mark by sixteen point six percent, while the institute's more sophisticated sample survey erred only by 0.3%.

stories.topic: The Bharat Sadhu Samaaj: Licensing Holy Men
stories.summary: In the mid-1950s there were an estimated 75 lakh sadhus in India, and the worry was that many were frauds. A sadhu registration bill was brought in 1956. To be recognised as a sadhu you would apply for a government licence and join the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj. President Rajendra Prasad then addressed the gathered sadhus. He told them nothing could be achieved in the other world without first setting this world in order, which was a pitch for their support of the Five-Year Plan. Amit found the story in Nikhil Menon's Planning Democracy.
stories.insight: The planning era's ambition reached as far as certifying holy men and recruiting them to sell the Plan. It is a vivid, comic picture of how far the planning state tried to extend.
stories.quote: He wanted the support for the five year plan because he said that you wanna be good in that world, you gotta be good in this world. Five year plan will get you there.

stories.topic: Haldane Moved to India to Stop Wearing Socks
stories.summary: JBS Haldane came to work at ISI in the mid-1950s, when he was in his sixties. He quipped that Mahalanobis's constant travels 'define a novel random vector'. Asked why he had left England for India, he didn't talk about simple living or escaping convention. He said he didn't want to wear socks anymore. Photos from the rest of his life show him in banyan, dhoti and pyjama, and never in socks.
stories.insight: This is Amit's favourite example of the writing principle 'show, don't tell': one concrete detail conveys a whole philosophy of life.
stories.quote: Instead, he said, I don't want to wear socks anymore. And that's such a beautiful sentiment because everybody immediately gets a vibe.

stories.topic: Chintaman Deshmukh's Proposal on a Tree
stories.summary: Around 1944 Chintaman Deshmukh, a senior official who later became finance minister, approved funding that practically guaranteed ISI's survival. Nikhil Menon describes him as a Cambridge-educated man who topped the Indian Civil Service, recited Vedic shlokas for pleasure, translated Kalidasa's Meghaduta and quoted scripture in support of economic policy. Widowed in the early 1950s, he married Durgabai Deshmukh. She was a feisty, outspoken woman who had been married off as a child at eight and, at 14, refused to go through with the marriage. Her autobiography, Chintaman and I, opens with his proposal.
stories.insight: The official who saved the institute was also a romantic. As Amit puts it, even people who care about statistics and math have hearts.
stories.quote: Chintaman took me to a eucalyptus tree in his garden and inscribed two Sanskrit slokas on its bark. It was a proposal of marriage. I accepted and he kissed me.

core_ideas.explanation: Intelligence comes from people (HUMINT) or from intercepted signals and communications (SIGINT). Authoritarian regimes are especially exposed to human sources, because their obedient staff are often full of people who privately hate the ruler.
core_ideas.quote: One of the great lessons of history is that authoritarian tyrants have obedient regimes that are full of people who hate them.

core_ideas.concept: Estimators and Their Limit: Cramér-Rao and Rao-Blackwell
core_ideas.explanation: Statistics is the craft of designing, analysing and comparing estimators, which are formulas that infer unknowns like the total number of German tanks. The Cramér-Rao lower bound shows there is a theoretical limit on how good an estimator can be for a given model and data set. The Rao-Blackwell theorem is a method for making an estimator one step better. CR Rao worked out both in Calcutta, the first in 1943.
core_ideas.quote: So you can run and run and build better and better estimators, but you can't cross the Cramér-Rao lower bound.

core_ideas.explanation: A data set usually contains only the survivors: planes that made it home, funds that weren't shut down, tips that happened to be right. The units that died along the way are invisible. Before trusting the data, ask how it was generated and what is missing. Wald's armour advice and the cricket-tipster scam are two versions of the same trap.
core_ideas.quote: When you see the data set, you are seeing the survivors. There are many units of observation that died along the way and you don't get to see them. So it's always important to think more clearly about the source of the data rather than blindly using the data.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay warns that data analysis is too often treated as feeding data into software and reading off answers. Stories like the tank and bomber problems show that real insight comes from understanding the problem, using intuition and common sense.
core_ideas.quote: For too many people, statistics has become a mechanical process where you throw some data into some software package and you get some answers. And always and always it is important to preserve fundamental intuition and insight and common sense.

core_ideas.concept: From Theorems to Algorithms: Mathematical vs Computational Statistics
core_ideas.explanation: Mid-century statistics was mathematical statistics: estimators were closed-form formulas, analysed by proving theorems. From the 1970s, with innovations like Bradley Efron's bootstrap in 1979, an estimator could be an algorithm. That merged statistics with computer science and led to today's data science. India's statistics community, so strong in the old style, missed this shift.
core_ideas.quote: An estimator doesn't have to be a closed-form mathematical formula. An estimator can be an algorithm.

core_ideas.concept: Ramanujan vs Anand: Two Models of Indian Genius
core_ideas.explanation: Ramanujan was a self-taught prodigy who appeared despite deprivation, but Cambridge and GH Hardy turned him into a great mathematician, so that achievement belongs to Cambridge's ecosystem. Anand was largely built by an Indian chess ecosystem, and he then helped nurture the next generation, so that India's teenagers are now among the best in the world. CR Rao fits the Anand model: an ordinary student who flourished inside the ecosystem Mahalanobis built.
core_ideas.quote: CR Rao to me is a little more of an Anand story and not the Ramanujan story.

core_ideas.concept: Excellence Comes From Founders, Not Bureaucracies
core_ideas.explanation: ISI reached the world frontier before independence, with no government funding, because of one eccentric, driven founder. Ajay is sceptical of calls for more public-sector universities. In his view, India's state-funded research and teaching institutions, IITs included, have management problems that seem incompatible with quality. What creates excellence is individuals who build isolated centres of excellence.
core_ideas.quote: What you need is a Mahalanobis. What you need is that eccentric, confident, crazy, creative person. What you don't need is a government bureaucracy.

core_ideas.concept: Credit Depends on the Decency of Gatekeepers
core_ideas.explanation: Work done in India, then and now, is easily ignored or later claimed by others in the global mainstream. Rao's 1943 results entered the canon only because Ronald Fisher chose to recognise them, just as the Royal Society chose to give Wallace credit alongside Darwin. Recognition is not automatic. It depends on the fairness of the people who shape a field.
core_ideas.quote: We see this even today in the age of the internet. That when work is done in India, very often the global mainstream just ignores it.

core_ideas.explanation: High modernism is a two-part belief. First, scientists and engineers know what should be done. Second, that special claim on truth entitles them to coercive power over everyone else. Minds trained on controlled systems such as a mathematical model, an engineering project or one piece of software are unprepared for societies, which are full of the unknowable. Milton Friedman made the same point about mathematicians like Mahalanobis who turn to economic planning.
core_ideas.quote: If there is one great thing we have learned through the twentieth century, it is that high modernism works pretty badly.

core_ideas.concept: Measure the Right Thing: Lives per Factory Destroyed
core_ideas.explanation: The bombing problem flips once you change what you measure. Instead of asking how risky each flight is, you ask how many lives each factory destroyed costs. Flying low is deadlier per flight but far more accurate, so fewer crews die in total. Choosing the right objective turns a gut fear into a solvable estimation problem.
core_ideas.quote: So how many lives does it take to kill a factory? Not the subjective fear of a pilot going to 6,000 feet or 20,000 feet.

core_ideas.explanation: Mahalanobis and ISI were early champions of the random sample survey. In the 1944 Bengal jute contest, a sample survey came within 0.3% of the truth, while plot-by-plot counting was off by 16.6%, and the survey cost a tenth as much. A well-designed sample can be both more accurate and cheaper than counting everything.
core_ideas.quote: Even more conclusively, the sample survey cost only a tenth of the enumeration.

core_ideas.explanation: A core writing principle: rather than stating a point in abstract words, convey it through a concrete detail. Haldane could have said he wanted a simple life free of convention. Instead he said he didn't want to wear socks anymore, and everyone instantly understood.
core_ideas.quote: The writing principle show don't tell is just don't tell something in straight words, show it with something.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After the German Tank Problem, Amit offers the moral: 'The moral of the story is brigadiers lie to their girlfriends.' Ajay adds: 'Or that tanks don't lie.'
Ajay brings the gag back in the bombing story, listing the ways to check bomb damage: 'You have a spotter plane, you have local intelligence, you have the brigadier's girlfriend.'

Amit on Wald's wartime group: it was so brilliant that someone quipped 'Milton Friedman is the fourth smartest person in the room'. And because Wald lacked security clearance, the joke went that a secretary took away each sheet the moment he finished writing it.
After telling how Wald died in a plane crash in India, Amit adds: 'Milton Friedman would now be the third smartest man in the room, but not in a way he would have liked.'

Poker banter between the stories. Amit: 'You had a German tank story. I call you and I raise you with a British airplane story.' After Ajay's bombing story, Amit says: 'You raised me, so I will just fold.'
On Sourish Das naming the package after CR Rao, Amit says: 'We should have called the show CR Rao. Everything is CR Rao.'
When Ajay starts talking about Julia, Amit riffs on the famous lyric: 'As another Julia would say, the hills are alive with the sound of coding.'

After the story of India missing the boat on computational statistics, Amit says: 'We missed the boat on algorithms and what I'm worried about is that you and I will miss the boat on the YouTube algorithm.' He follows with a pun on going viral and Viral Shah, the Julia co-creator Ajay had just mentioned.
When cats start fighting off-camera, Amit tells viewers it is the 'ghosts of statisticians past who have worked at the ISI wailing to see the condition'.

Amit happily accepts Ajay's claim that CR Rao, from Andhra Pradesh, is the Bengal Renaissance's greatest achievement: 'You know the whole world is Bengali.' He mentions a fantasy novel in which Bengal colonizes the world, quotes the American Statistical Association's praise of Rao as a 'Bengal Renaissance man', and later declares: 'All Bengali geniuses are belong to me, Dada.'

After reading Nikhil Menon's portrait of a stern, prim Mahalanobis who showed affection only to dogs, cats and cows, Amit tells Ajay that apart from the dogs and cows, 'the rest of this seems to fit you'. Ajay replies: 'Cows also.'
On Mahalanobis making staff log their daily activities, Amit says to Ajay, the privacy advocate: 'he would have loved Aadhaar'.

On the government licensing sadhus, Ajay asks: 'Was there a certification examination? Was there a UID?' Amit trips over his words: 'Once the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj was farmed, formed, not farmed, you could farm them', with sadhus' 'documentation in triplicate'.

On Haldane and socks, Amit says nobody likes wearing socks 'unless they're kind of kinky and, you know, they wear it on their heads while doing unspeakable things. Look up autoerotic asphyxiation.' The show notes link the topic with the warning: '(Do not try this at home.)'
After the eucalyptus-tree proposal: 'when men were men and inscribed Sanskrit shlokas into barks of trees. Have you ever done that?' The answer: 'No, no such luck.'
Amit, a self-described man of the right, introduces his recommendation: 'I want to turn to my right because I'm always turning to the right.'
Amit quotes Haldane's line that Mahalanobis's constant travels 'define a novel random vector', then admits: 'I have no idea what that phrase means, but I'm sure you do.'

'Coming back on a wing and a prayer': Ajay calls it one of the most beautiful phrases in English and traces it to WWII bombers whose engines were shot out, gliding home on just a wing and hoping to make it.
Ricky Ponting on becoming a great batsman, quoted by Amit as an intuitive version of Wald's insight: 'Most batsmen have a map of the fielders in their head. I had a map of the gaps.'

Darwin and Wallace: Ajay compares the joint names on Rao's theorems to the 'Darwin-Wallace theory of evolution'. The Royal Society gave both men credit, even though Wallace had his idea in a malaria fever dream weeks earlier while Darwin had been working on it for decades.
Sankhya, the journal ISI built in its golden age, was respected as world-class, and 'libraries all over the world would get Sankhya'.

The American Statistical Association on CR Rao, quoted by Amit: 'Rao is a living legend whose work has influenced not just statistics, but has far-reaching implications for fields as varied as economics, genetics, anthropology, geology, national planning, demography, biometry, and medicine.'

Milton Friedman on Mahalanobis, quoted by Amit: able mathematicians, 'working in a field of absolutes', become dangerous in economic planning because 'they produce specific and detailed plans in which they have confidence without perhaps realizing that economic planning is not the absolute science that mathematics is.'
